title: Alpha–Theta Training
subtitle: State-based training often used with eyes closed
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating alpha–theta training within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain alpha–theta training without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in alpha–theta training.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to alpha–theta training.

sections.explainSimply: Alpha–theta protocols usually provide feedback while the person rests deeply and tracks changing slower rhythms.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: They are sometimes used for trauma, substance use or performance, but procedures and theoretical models vary substantially.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Screen for dissociation, destabilisation, psychosis risk, seizure history and tolerance of reduced external orientation. Evidence remains limited and protocol-dependent.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Choosing a camera lens: every method emphasises some information and introduces its own distortions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand alpha–theta training to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Deep relaxation is not universally safe or therapeutic.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using alpha–theta training predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Deep relaxation is not universally safe or therapeutic. Evidence classification: insufficient to mixed evidence.
